reading.body:
Vermont has 64 AI-related bills in this dataset, and the largest cluster regulates data centers and the power and land they need. Two bills name the physical constraint directly: S0205 proposes a temporary moratorium on AI data centers and a report on their construction and operation, and H0727 addresses sustainable data center deployment. H0720 goes further and reframes cloud computing as a public utility. This is the compute layer of AI policy, and in Vermont it is being treated as a siting and utility question rather than a model question.

The second cluster is liability and disclosure. H0792 sets liability standards for developers and deployers, H0341 creates oversight and safety standards for inherently dangerous systems, H0855 defines defenses in civil actions for AI-caused harm, and H0822 regulates generative systems. A third cluster covers specific uses: mental health services, health care coverage decisions, chatbots and companion chatbots, elections and synthetic media, employment decisions, rental housing pricing, and automated decision systems. The bills span January 2025 through May 2026, with the heaviest concentration in January 2026.

What the data does not show is enactment. Every entry is a bill with a number and a date, and the dataset carries no status field, so nothing here says which of the 64 became law. It also does not quantify Vermont's data center load, its electricity prices, or its interconnection queue, so the strength of the power constraint in Vermont specifically cannot be read from this list. The single news item, from September 2026, reports governors broadly uneasy about AI, which is context rather than evidence about Vermont.
